A tarantula is a very large, hairy spider. It belongs to a family of spiders called Theraphosidae, and it is one of the biggest spiders in the world. When most people think of a giant, intimidating spider, the tarantula is usually what comes to mind.
What Does It Look Like?

A tarantula has the same basic body plan as any spider — eight legs, two main body parts (the front section with the head, and the rounded rear section), two fang-like mouthparts (called chelicerae), and eight eyes.

What makes tarantulas stand out is their size and their thick covering of hair. These hairs aren't just for looks — they serve important purposes, which we'll get to shortly.

In terms of size, tarantulas vary quite a bit. A smaller tarantula might have a leg span of about 7–8 cm (roughly 3 inches). The largest species — the Goliath birdeater, found in South America — can have a leg span of up to 30 cm (nearly 12 inches) and weigh as much as 170 grams. It is the largest spider in the world by body mass.
Where Do They Live?

Tarantulas are found on every continent except Antarctica. They are especially common in:

  • Tropical rainforests (South America, Southeast Asia, Africa)
  • Deserts and dry scrublands (American Southwest, parts of Africa and Australia)
  • Grasslands and forests around the world

Many species dig burrows underground, where they spend most of their time. Others live in trees (these are called arboreal tarantulas) and build silken retreats in hollow trunks or among branches. Some species simply hide under rocks, logs, or leaf litter.
How Do They Hunt?

Tarantulas are predators — they hunt and eat other animals. They do not spin webs to catch prey the way common garden spiders do. Instead, they are ambush hunters: they wait patiently near the entrance of their burrow or hiding spot, and when something edible wanders too close, they pounce on it quickly.

They use their fangs to grab the prey and inject venom, which both paralyzes the animal and begins to break down its insides. Because spiders cannot chew solid food, the tarantula then drinks the liquefied contents of its prey.
What Do They Eat?

The main diet of a tarantula consists of:

  • Insects (crickets, grasshoppers, beetles, moths)
  • Other invertebrates (millipedes, other spiders)

Larger species are capable of taking down bigger prey, including:

  • Small lizards and frogs
  • Mice and small rats
  • Small birds (this happens very rarely in the wild, but it did give the Goliath birdeater its dramatic name — an old illustration once depicted one eating a bird)
Are They Venomous? Are They Dangerous?

Yes, all tarantulas are venomous. However, for most species, their venom is not seriously dangerous to humans. A bite from most tarantulas feels roughly like a bee sting — painful and sometimes accompanied by localized swelling, redness, or nausea, but not life-threatening for a healthy adult.

That said, there are important distinctions between two broad groups:

New World tarantulas (found in North and South America) tend to have milder venom. Their main defense against threats is a clever trick: they use their back legs to flick tiny, barbed hairs from their abdomen toward an attacker. These hairs, called urticating hairs, are extremely irritating to skin, eyes, and the throat of predators. If you've ever gotten these hairs on your skin or in your eyes, it causes intense itching and irritation that can last hours or days.

Old World tarantulas (found in Africa, Asia, Europe, and Australia) do not have urticating hairs. As a result, they tend to be more defensive and quick to bite when threatened, and their venom is generally more potent.

For people who are allergic, any tarantula bite can potentially trigger a serious allergic reaction, in the same way a bee sting can be dangerous to someone with an allergy. But outside of allergic reactions, tarantula bites are generally not medically severe.
How Do They Grow?

Like all spiders, tarantulas have a hard outer shell (called an exoskeleton) instead of an internal skeleton. Because this shell cannot grow, a tarantula must shed it entirely in a process called molting (or ecdysis) in order to grow larger.

During a molt, the tarantula flips onto its back, splits its old shell open, and slowly wriggles out of it — revealing a new, soft shell underneath, which then hardens over the following days. During this period, the tarantula is extremely vulnerable because its body is soft and its fangs cannot be used properly.

One remarkable thing about molting: if a tarantula has lost a leg (from an injury or a predator attack), it can regenerate it during a molt. The new leg may look slightly smaller than the others at first but grows back to full size over successive molts.

Young tarantulas molt several times a year. Adults molt much less frequently — perhaps once a year or even less.
How Long Do They Live?

Tarantulas are exceptionally long-lived for spiders — among the longest-lived of all arachnids.

  • Females can live anywhere from 20 to over 30 years, depending on the species.
  • Males, unfortunately, have far shorter lives. Once a male reaches sexual maturity, he typically lives only another 1–3 years. After mating, males often die shortly afterward — and in some cases, the female will actually eat the male.

This is one reason why female tarantulas are more commonly kept as pets.
How Do They Use Silk?

Unlike web-building spiders, tarantulas use their silk differently:

  • To line their burrows, making them smoother and more stable
  • To create tripwire threads around the entrance of their burrow — when an insect walks across these threads, the vibrations alert the tarantula that prey is nearby
  • To build egg sacs to protect their eggs
  • To help anchor themselves while climbing, so they don't fall
Reproduction

When a male tarantula matures, he goes on a search for a female, often traveling surprisingly long distances. Before approaching, he uses special structures on his front legs (called palps) to deposit sperm, then transfers it to the female during mating.

After a successful mating, the female produces an egg sac made of silk, which can contain anywhere from a few dozen to over a thousand eggs depending on the species. She guards this sac carefully until the spiderlings hatch.
Tarantulas as Pets

Tarantulas are one of the most popular exotic pets in the world. They are relatively low-maintenance compared to dogs or cats — they don't need daily feeding, they don't make noise, and they require modest space. Most pet owners keep them in terrariums with appropriate substrate (material for burrowing), a small water dish, and controlled humidity and temperature suited to their natural habitat.

Popular pet species include:

  • The Mexican red-knee (Brachypelma hamorii) — known for its striking orange-red "knee" patches and calm temperament
  • The Chilean rose (Grammostola rosea) — extremely docile and commonly recommended for beginners
  • The Brazilian black (Grammostola pulchra) — entirely jet-black and known for a gentle disposition
A Common Misunderstanding

Despite their fierce appearance, tarantulas are generally shy and reclusive animals. In the wild, they almost always try to retreat or use their urticating hairs as a first response rather than biting. A bite is usually a last resort.

Their fearsome reputation is largely a product of their size and appearance rather than their actual danger level. Many experienced keepers find them to be calm, fascinating animals that are far less aggressive than their looks suggest.
In Short

A tarantula is a very large, hairy spider found across much of the world's warmer regions. It is a venomous but generally non-lethal predator that hunts by ambush, lives for a surprisingly long time (especially females), sheds its entire outer shell to grow, and uses silk in clever ways without spinning a traditional web. While intimidating in appearance, most tarantulas are not particularly dangerous to humans and are widely kept as exotic pets.
